stem: A reactive agent is best described by which of the following behaviors?

options.text: It maintains a detailed internal model of future states before acting
It maps its current perception directly to an action via fixed condition-action rules, with no lookahead
It always takes longer to respond than a deliberative agent
It requires a multi-agent system to function

explanation.why_correct: A reactive agent's defining trait is a direct mapping from current perception to action using fixed condition-action rules, without building or reasoning over an internal model of future states.

why_incorrect.A: Maintaining and reasoning over an internal model of future states is the defining trait of a deliberative agent, not a reactive one.
why_incorrect.C: Reactive agents are typically FASTER than deliberative agents, since they skip the planning/lookahead step entirely.
why_incorrect.D: Reactive agents can operate as single, standalone agents; nothing about the reactive architecture requires a multi-agent setup.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Reactive = direct perception-to-action mapping, no internal world model, no lookahead -- and typically fast as a result.

stem: An agent is asked to plan a multi-city trip itinerary that satisfies several budget and scheduling constraints, considering multiple candidate itineraries before choosing the best one. Which agent architecture does this best exemplify?

options.text: Hybrid, purely because more than one city is involved
Reactive, since the trip request is a single input
Neither, since trip planning cannot be done by any agent architecture
Deliberative, since it builds and reasons over an internal model of candidate plans and their consequences

explanation.why_correct: Evaluating multiple candidate itineraries against constraints before choosing the best one is precisely the planning-ahead, consequence-weighing behavior that characterizes a deliberative agent.

why_incorrect.B: Having a single input request does not make the underlying decision-making reactive; what matters is whether the agent plans ahead and weighs alternatives, which it clearly does here.
why_incorrect.C: Trip planning is a well-established example task for deliberative planning approaches; it is very much within the capability of deliberative agent architectures.
why_incorrect.A: The number of cities involved has no bearing on whether the architecture is hybrid; hybrid specifically means combining a fast reactive layer with a slower deliberative layer, which is not described here.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Weighing multiple candidate plans against constraints before committing is a hallmark of deliberative reasoning, regardless of how many entities (cities, items) are involved.

stem: A customer support system first tries to match an incoming ticket against a list of common, well-known issues using fast pattern matching. If no confident match is found, it escalates the ticket to a more expensive, extended reasoning process. What type of architecture is this?

options.text: Purely reactive, since pattern matching is involved
Purely deliberative, since reasoning is eventually used
Hybrid, combining a fast reactive layer with a selectively-invoked deliberative layer
Multi-agent, since there are two separate processing stages

explanation.why_correct: This design combines a fast reactive-style pattern-matching layer for common cases with a slower deliberative reasoning layer invoked only when the fast path is insufficient -- exactly the hybrid architecture pattern of selective escalation.

why_incorrect.A: The system is not purely reactive, since it has an escalation path to deliberative reasoning for cases that don't match confidently.
why_incorrect.B: The system is not purely deliberative either, since the common case is handled by fast pattern matching without full deliberation.
why_incorrect.D: Having two processing stages within one system does not make it a multi-agent system; multi-agent systems involve multiple distinct agents, which is a different architectural concept from layered single-agent processing.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Fast-path-first with selective escalation to slower, more thorough reasoning is the defining signature of a hybrid architecture, not a multi-agent system or a purely single-mode design.

stem: A team is building a system for real-time video game NPC behavior that must respond within milliseconds to player actions, where most situations are well-understood and recurring. Which architecture is most appropriate, and why?

options.text: Deliberative, because games always benefit from the most sophisticated architecture available
Reactive, because the task demands fast responses to mostly familiar, recurring situations
Hybrid, because all production systems must be hybrid
It is impossible to choose without knowing the game's graphics engine

explanation.why_correct: A millisecond-level response requirement combined with mostly familiar, recurring situations is exactly the profile that favors a reactive architecture, since there is little time for and little benefit from deliberation in this context.

why_incorrect.A: Architecture choice should be driven by task and environment properties (speed needs, novelty), not a blanket preference for the most sophisticated-sounding option -- deliberation would likely be too slow here.
why_incorrect.C: Hybrid is not a universal requirement for production systems; the appropriate choice depends on the specific task's time-sensitivity and novelty profile, which here clearly favors pure reactivity.
why_incorrect.D: The graphics engine is unrelated to the agent-architecture decision, which depends on response-time requirements and situation familiarity, not rendering technology.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Millisecond-level response requirements combined with mostly familiar situations point clearly toward a reactive architecture -- deliberation's extra robustness isn't worth its latency cost here.

stem: What is the primary tradeoff between reactive and deliberative agent architectures?

options.text: Deliberative agents never make mistakes
Reactive agents can never be implemented using language models
Reactive agents are faster but less robust on novel situations; deliberative agents are more robust but slower and more computationally expensive
There is no meaningful tradeoff; one architecture is strictly better in all cases

explanation.why_correct: The core tradeoff is speed/simplicity versus robustness/cost: reactive agents respond quickly but can struggle with novel situations outside their rule set, while deliberative agents handle novelty and multi-step problems better at the cost of more computation and latency per decision.

why_incorrect.B: Language models can readily implement reactive behavior (e.g. a quick, low-effort response with no planning); the reactive/deliberative distinction is about architecture, not about which underlying technology is used.
why_incorrect.D: There is a genuine, well-documented tradeoff between the two approaches; neither is strictly superior across all tasks and environments.
why_incorrect.A: Deliberative agents can still make mistakes, particularly if their internal model of the world is inaccurate or their planning process has flaws; deliberation improves robustness but is not an error-elimination guarantee.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: The reactive-vs-deliberative tradeoff is speed and simplicity versus robustness and cost -- the right choice depends on the task, not a universal ranking.

stem: A reactive agent built with a fixed set of condition-action rules encounters an input situation that does not clearly match any of its rules. What is the most likely outcome, given the architecture's inherent limitations?

options.text: The agent will automatically invent a sound new rule through internal deliberation
The agent is likely to respond poorly or unpredictably, since it has no deeper reasoning process to fall back on for unmatched situations
The agent will seamlessly switch itself into a deliberative architecture
The agent will always correctly default to asking a clarifying question

explanation.why_correct: Handling novel situations that fall outside the predefined rule set is a well-known limitation of reactive architectures, since by design there is no deeper deliberation process to reason through an unfamiliar case -- the typical outcome is a poor or unpredictable response.

why_incorrect.A: Inventing new rules through deliberation is a deliberative capability, not something a reactive architecture does by definition -- a purely reactive agent has no such reasoning process available.
why_incorrect.C: A reactive agent does not spontaneously become a different architecture; architecture is a design-time property, not something the system changes on its own at runtime.
why_incorrect.D: There is no guarantee a reactive agent defaults to asking a clarifying question for unmatched input -- its behavior in that case depends entirely on whatever fallback rule (if any) was predefined, which may or may not be a clarifying question.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: A reactive agent facing a situation outside its rule set has no deeper reasoning to fall back on -- this is the core limitation that distinguishes reactive from deliberative design.
